description_full: ePlus inc., together with its subsidiaries, provides information technology (IT) solutions that enable organizations to optimize IT environment and supply chain processes in the United States and internationally. The company operates through three segments: Product Services, Professional Services, and Managed Services segments. It sells third-party hardware, perpetual and subscription software, and maintenance; and software assurance and other third-party services as well as offers internet-based business-to-business supply chain management solutions for IT products. The company also offers professional services, such as staff augmentation, project management, cloud consulting, Al advisory, consulting, security and collaboration solution, warehouse, configuration, and logistic service, as well as in the spaces of digital signage, EV charging solution, loss prevention and security, store opening, remodel, and store closing; and managed services comprising enhanced maintenance support or ePlus Lifecycle-Services Support, service desk, storage-as-a-service, azure recover, cloud managed, and managed security service, as well as managed service for infrastructure and cloud. It serves telecommunications, media and entertainment, technology, state and local government, educational institutions, healthcare, and financial services. The company was formerly known as MLC Holdings, Inc. and changed its name to ePlus inc. in 1999. ePlus inc. was founded in 1990 and is headquartered in Herndon, Virginia.
ceo_bio: Mr. Mark P. Marron | CEO, President & Director | Age 63 | Compensation: $3.7M (FY2026)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 2K people. Revenue per employee of $1.1M ranks in the top quartile among Technology peers, improving at 7%/yr — growing workforce leverage. Stock-based compensation of $6K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 3× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (3/10).
financial_summary: ePlus inc. is a mid-cap technology business with a $2.4B market cap on $2.4B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +6% over the past three years and +7% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.

Returns on capital run at 19% against a 10% cost of capital — a 9-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, and 25% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.
The company is burning through $121M of cash, and without positive owner earnings any valuation rests on hope rather than evidence.
Accruals are elevated at +13.8% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.
Shareholder yield is only 1.9%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 2.2% of the shares, and profit capture is only 0.3× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sect: Its 7% operating margin is roughly in line with the Technology median (7%).
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.29x its revenue share).
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-8.8% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 530 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 30% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 8% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 6% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 35% and a beta of 1.01, it moves roughly with the market.
About $17.9M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 48% in the 2020 crash, 32% in the 2022 bear market and 42% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its blended-model fair value of $81.78 (margin of safety -13%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 32%), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Technology peers: P/E 19.8 vs 26.7 and EV/EBITDA 9.7 vs 16.4 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 9% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of -5.0% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 8.7% (vs the 8% bar).
The Street target $111 on average, 21% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 19% clears the cost of capital of 9.8% by 9pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have been steady (CV 0.14).
It runs a 25% gross margin and burns cash (FCF margin -5%).
Earnings quality is a concern: cash conversion of only -0.88x and high accruals (+13.8% of assets).
ROE of 12% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.7x equity multiplier).
It spends 0.5% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $271.5M.
Warning signs: a Beneish M-score that flags possible earnings manipulation, which caps the rating at HOLD.
Its debt comes due soon (maturity wall about 0.9 years out), so refinancing terms matter.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 5.7% over 3 years, 9.3% over 5 years and 7.3% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 18.5% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.00, a backlog worth 0% of annual revenue and deferred revenue up 64%.
Capex runs only 0.2x depreciation (0.2% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 4, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own a modest 2.2%, and institutions hold 98%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (25 sales, net $1.9M sold).
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.9% (1.1% in buybacks and 1.2% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 0.7% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
people: With about 2,148 employees, each generates about $1.1M of revenue, 3.1x the Technology median, and productivity has risen 7.5% a year.
Free cash flow is negative, at -$56K per employee.
CEO pay is $3.7M (3x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
